blocks.x: I'll put down the date on here. It's March the 16th, 1961, and we're at the home of Mr. Dalton Richards, is that right? That's right. Could you give your full name? Do you have any middle initial or middle name? Dalton E. Richards. Do you mind telling just when you were born and where it was? May 27th, 1908. What part of the city was right here in New Orleans? At 2519 Second Street. Uptown. Could you tell us anything about your early music experience? Did your mother and father play any instrument or sing or have any music in your home?

My mother played, my older sister played, and my sister, the next to the older sister, played... What instrument? Piano. My oldest brother played piano. My next to the oldest brother played piano. Uh, my brother George, he played trumpet. Oh, somebody wants to see. I'll turn it off for a minute.
See, you were telling about all your family played piano. You had a piano right in your home then.

That's it. And, uh, the history of that piano, that piano, most of us learned on that one piano. I got rid of that piano in 1963. That's not so long ago now. Well, how long did you have it then? That piano stayed in the family. They bought that piano before I was born.
Oh, yeah. Because my sister— Four nineteen and eight then?

Yes. My sister, it was a Sharma. And it was a heavy thing, and when we moved on Broadway Street in the house, it was too heavy to bring up stairs, so we left it in the basement. And I used to play it, and practice on it, and play it, and practice on it, until the strings couldn't stand anymore. They told me the only thing that'd be done, left to be done with the piano was to have it restrown. I thought it was too expensive. Yeah. I sold it for $25. Sold it for $25. And get settled. Now, my youngest sister is a nun. She's been from Juilliard. Oh, really? She had a dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear She's teaching my little girl music now, and she's a genius. And it was through her, when she was going to school at Xavier, after I left Xavier, around 1925, she was really stuck with the music. And so I started following her, and she started helping me a little bit. So the whole family knew Steve Lewis.
Oh yes. I never got to hear him, but I knew all that I played with Theron.

Well, my oldest brother was a good friend of Steve. They were good buddies. So I went to Steve and asked Steve would he help me. By the way, what was your older brother's name? Edwin Richards. Edwin. Is he still living? Yes, he's still living. Is he still...
The one you said played trumpet?
No, George. My brother George played the trumpet. Oh, he's still living, too. But he doesn't play, he doesn't play anymore. He played for about three years, and he quit.
I knew. Yes. If you wanted... We can turn off for a minute. We're talking about your brother, your oldest brother Edwin.
Yes, who was helping me with what he knew. And he told me to go over and see Steve Lewis. And she asked Steve would he help me. And they also knew Joe Robichaux. Oh, yeah.
I just rode the bus down at the Joe Robichaux.
Yeah. Well, Joe and Steve, they helped me. And that's how I learned to play the piano. And I learned how to read little music from my sister while she was learning.

Well, I think of it, excuse the interruption, would your brother be willing to give us an interview sometime, too? Do you think he would have any interest in music anymore? Would he mind talking about the old days? No.
No, he wasn't. He wasn't a musician. He played mostly for entertainer amongst the group, you know. He didn't play out like I do. It was fun to be able to.

He didn't play out like I do. Steve Lewis, if he maybe knew a good deal about Steve, maybe more than, as I say, we've heard of him a lot. Everybody talks about him a little bit, but nobody's really told us much about his life or how he played.

Well, I'd like to talk to my brother Edwin and find out if he could give an interview, if he could think about the time we had with Steve. Even a half an hour or so. Yeah, even a half an hour or so, you know. Because Steve was their buddy. They were partly raised together. And, uh, Steve was a great piano player. One of the greatest. I mean, and, uh, he helped Joe Robichaux and Joe Robichaux helped me. I, uh...
Well, what type of piano did your mother play? Was it classical or any popular music or what kind of...

Well, as I understood, she played for a while and then she gave it up. She played classical, mostly just classical, you know, out of the... You know, methodical. Method books, yes. My sister Stella, she played out of the Method books. My sister Edna, well, she was a school teacher. She would play out of the Method books. She would play all her little school songs and everything for the children, you know. But, uh, the best musician in the family would be my sister Marie, who, yes. You have to give it to her because she's...she's a genius. She has a...a choir over at St. Mary's Academy. An a cappella choir. I wish you could hear her sing. And, uh, she trains choral groups and she has a lot of students over there taking...that are all taking piano lessons under her, you know. But, in the meantime, I kept on fooling around while I was playing around, playing around, playing around, playing around. I learned how to play. Going to Joe Wilbyshire's house. He was right around the corner from me. And, uh, eventually I started out. I was hired to play at these house parties.
Oh, yeah.

Well, the money wasn't much, but the fun was there, you understand? And they had, uh, at that time about two or three fellas that were doing the same thing. We played house parties. If it wasn't...if it wasn't me, it was Craig. A fella named James Craig. He was a piano player.
But how old were you when you started playing at those parties?
Well, I'd say around 1927.
Another 19-something.

And, uh, they had another fella, uh, Henry Wilkeson. We all used to play for house parties. If they didn't hire me, they'd hire Craig or Henry. Well, I kept on playing, kept on playing, kept on playing. So one of the fellas asked me, why don't I start playing with a band? And then, uh, he was playing with a band. So I told him, but I didn't know too much about the music. He said, well, you can read that orchestrate. If you practice, you know enough about, uh, the piano and everything. If you try, you can make it. So my brother, George, my brother Edwin played bass in the little band. bass in the little band. Arthur Cleese, Charles Fletcher, he's dead. What did he play? He played guitar.
Oh.

Elwood Thedover, he played saxophone. Arthur Cleese played saxophone. And I played the piano. Well that was around the time when this number Blue Skies came out. Oh yeah, Earthenbelly, isn't it? Earthenbelly is not. We had the band then. And we used to rehearse two or three times a week. We played two or three jobs at little dance halls and things like that, nothing notable, you know, just people would hire the band, we played for a couple of weddings, a couple of birthday parties. And so after they disbanded, well I stopped playing a while. And I saw Joe and Joe asked me, why didn't I stop? Why did I stop? Well I just thought over, because things are going to get better. So I met some fellas that was there, this was around 1932 or 1934, during the Depression, and the musicians weren't making any money. Yeah, well, I don't know that one. See? They had that WPA band that you were playing in that band? Yeah, I didn't play in that. No, I didn't play in that, because they didn't use the piano to play in that band. No, just not. No. Now, a lot of the fellas in the band, I knew, I knew most of them. But Howard Davis, and Alvin Alcorn, George Williams, the drummer, and myself, we played a little job on Irada, or no, Clio and Clonelet. A little night spot there, and we started playing Friday, Saturdays, and Sundays. Friday, Saturdays, and Sundays. But I mean, the money wasn't enough, I mean, I didn't like it, I was working, I mean, at that time, you know, I didn't like that type of life. Yeah. When you played the parties, what did they pay for those? Sometimes you make five dollars a night. Most of the time it was three dollars.
They just paid you a flat sum, you didn't get tips or anything at the party?

No, no tips. No tips. Now, when we would play some of, for some of the white people, you'd make tips. Sometimes a fellow would actually play Satan numbers, they wanted all the old numbers that you could think of, like after the ball was over, down by the old mill stream, so they could get a, what you would call a drunken chord group around the piano and all the things. And later on, I found out that that did benefit me by me knowing those numbers, because one time I played for, or some people, I forget who they were, but by playing those numbers, I made about twenty-five dollars extra that night. I forgot where it was. I played all those old numbers, I mean, all the numbers that you could think of back from in the eighteen, in the nineteenth century. And they'd ask me, did I know this? And they'd ask me, did they start singing the melody to me? And I had a very, very ear I could play, and I could improvise pretty well, you see? But those house parties we played for then, we wouldn't make much. Did you sing the number six of that party? Yeah, I would sing. Yes, I'd sing. But now, the time came when I gave it up for a while. And up until the forties, I had that piano in the house. Very something I would touch it. Around nineteen forty-five, I moved next door to Albert French. And I used to practice and play, and practice and play. He said, Dalton, why don't you start playing again, man? I said, get to working out there and make you some nice money. Join the union? I said, oh man, there's nothing in it. He said, well, let's try. So, I kept on playing, practicing, and something like that. And he said, look, man, we need a piano player on a little job we're going up there. It's not my job, it's Eugene Boyd's job. You want to try it? I said, yeah, I'll try it. So, I went out with him that Saturday night. And from that when I started again. That was in 1945.

Yeah, I'm trying to think, who's Eugene Boyd? I can't remember. He's a tennis saxophone player. Tennis sax. I knew, I didn't know him, but I was George Boyd. George Boyd, they called him George Boyd. The clarinet player way back. But, uh, I know a lot of people worked with him. I didn't know him personally.

No. I know George Boyd, he called him. George Boyd. I remember him. He's an old, old musician. Yeah, he did. Uh-huh. He played, I think he played that old Eureka band, if he was saying George Boyd, I'm thinking about.
Yeah, probably he did. He played a lot of the bands. I know Lee Collins told me he used to be, you know, George Lewis, he learned a lot of things. Yeah, yeah. It was interesting to him, too.

Well, uh, he's an older man in Georgia. Yeah, he was before him. Uh-huh. So, uh, we started playing nightclubs. And I enjoyed it. And Albert Frenchy, who was in with Celestan, and when Papa would have two jobs the same night that he couldn't fulfill, well, he'd get a very good Dixieland trumpet player, like Alvin Alcorn or somebody, and, or another trombone player we call, Showboyd.
I can't think of Showboyd's name, but he was a good... I can't think of it, Alvin.

He's a good trombone player. He's a Dixieland trombone player. And, uh, we had Sidney Montague on drums, Howard Davis on trumpet, I mean on saxophone, alto sax and clarinet, Alvin Alcorn on trumpet, Alvin Alcorn was playing, would play banjo and guitar. See? When he played those Dixieland jobs, he used his banjo. And he really could sing, see? So, I mean, at that time I began liking it. One time we went to one of Celestan's jobs, he couldn't fulfill the engagement, so he asked Albert to take charge. We went to St. Francisville. And they had a very, very big auction up there. I forgot the name of the man. The man is Mr. Cobb, I believe. I think that he has a farm of Van St. Francisville. Well, they had an auction there. I read in the paper the very next day that it was around $300 and some other thousand dollars of cattle that sold. They had cattlemen from all over the country, Oklahoma. Where is that about? I don't remember. St. Francisville. It's above Baton Rouge. Up above, up near the river, is it? Yeah. This old plantation town. And we went up there that night, and we played. We were supposed to play to twelve, but we had to play to about two, because that's one of the nights they had Albert singing and me playing all those old numbers. And Albert would pick them up as I tried, Lazy Jane and everything like that, that's what they wanted. And we, he satisfied them, so we made pretty good tips. We made, at an average of about fifteen dollars a minute extra tips at a six piece band.
Oh, I see. Sure boy, is his name Worthy Thomas? Worthy Thomas. That's it, Worthy Thomas. I couldn't think of that. You sure know, he doesn't Worthy Thomas. That's it.

Took me a long time to think of it. Yeah. Now, he was with us on that job up there at St. Francisville. Yeah. And, I mean, we, we just kept on going from place to place like that, until I started getting jobs when I got around two lanes. See, I used to play the twelve hundred Broadway. That's Sigma 58. Fraternity, yeah. Yeah. The Delta Fire on the 25-14 state. 1471, Henry Clay. 1036, Ottomans. 1018, Ottomans. Ten... What did you do? 800 Ottomans. I can't think of all the names.
It was Saturday night parties. They had night parties.

They had night parties. Especially during the rush week. We used to be busy every night. And, uh, we had the same group with Albert French, Howard Davis, Alvin Alcon, and, uh, Sidney Montaguey on the drums. And very similar, we used a bass, but that was usually a five-piece band. We had a little, a good five-piece band. We could play any kind of music that people wanted. If they wanted Dixieland, we could play that. And, uh, if they wanted any kind of music, we could play it. Now, Al- Howard Davis left town, and he went to California. I met him out there two years ago. Uh-huh. And, uh, we started using, uh, Parnell. We were lucky to get him. Oh, yeah. Between his six bells. Alton. Is it, uh, Alton Parnell is...
He's a piano player. No, not here. He's a brother.

No, no. Man, that guy was a saxophone player, a supreme. I mean, he, he gave the incentive to play. And I used to like to hire him. And sometimes I'd use, uh, Son Johnson, that's George Johnson, and Parnell together. Well, that's two of the best saxophone players in the city, see? And we had Al, Alvin Alcon, and Alvin French singing, and had a little fella called Jim Davis on the bass. But we had, I always did bring up there, a good outfit for those boys, and they were very well pleased, you see? And, uh, during the time I was playing like that, Miss Neda St. Paul, that was George St. Paul's daughter before she married. All her little cocktail parties she used to give on Phillip Street there. We played a couple of houses over there, too. Just the piano. And I went there a couple times by myself, so I thought I'd bring somebody to help me sing, so I brought Albert French. And we played about five or six parties for the St. Paul's. Well, that's in that, what they call the Garden District section. Yeah, pretty houses in there. Yeah. And, uh, they liked our music. They'd call me anytime, sometimes, nine or ten o'clock, asking where'd I come play for them. I told them, sure. And I'd just play the job around, and those people, that's one thing about those people, those kind of people, they would ask you how much you owe them. I'd always tell them, give me what they want, because I knew I'd be well paid, you know. Sometimes thirty dollars, sometimes forty dollars. People would just have the money to pay. They'd ask me if it was enough, because, you know, it was enough for three or four hours playing, see? So, we lost Albert. Papa Sellers, yeah. So, he would always throw jobs our way when Papa would have two jobs.

By the way, Alvin Alcorn is working with that group now again. Yeah, he is. They don't have Fernandes anymore. No. Albert's finances quit? Well, I don't know. There's some, maybe a disagreement or something, and so they're using Alvin at present. Well, I tell you. For some time now, a few weeks or months at least, here.

You know, he lives up on my rod, and I know he, I see him pretty often. I always see his family. He is a good trumpet player, yet. I mean, usually the trumpet players' lips go bad, you know. But he is a good trumpet player, and he's a nice fellow to be around. Some of the musicians, you don't care about being around, I have to admit. That's right. He's a wonderful fellow. He is a nice fellow. Albert French had one of the best dispositions for musicians. It's always a grill. He's always a grill. I mean, anywhere you'd go, we went to Biloxi with him, one of the Celestane's job, went to the Gulfport on Celestane's job with him. Celestane must have had two engagements that night, you know, so Albert would take the other one. But our kind of band we'd bring, honestly, I mean, it was a better band if it was the Papa than Celestane had, but people wanted Papa because of Papa. He had a big name, yeah. And we had better, yeah, we had Alvin Alcorn, guys like that, that's the girl, and he went away and he was playing with Kidora and those people.
Yeah, right. Went to Europe with him about two years, three years ago.
And we played around, we would job around, place to place. A couple of nights we went into Fuqa Radio. Well, I don't like that, I'm going to be frank. I mean, I work in the post office, I have a job.
I was going to ask about the post office, I noticed the insignia on your arm, you mentioned your route.

Yeah. How long have you been with the post office? Since 1940. 21 years old, man. Yeah, yeah, yeah. And playing in the Fuqa Radio, most of the jobs out there start at nine and you play until three. Well, I mean, that wouldn't be six hours of playing, you play 40 and you dress 20.
Yeah.
But if you have to have a job like I had and you have to go to work the next day, you wouldn't care much for that.
No. No.

So I tried it a couple of Tuesday nights because I was off on Wednesday. But I lost my Wednesday because I had to sleep almost all day because you play that far to me. Yeah. You don't play like you play. You play far to me. And that's hard.
Which place were you playing?
We went to the Mardi Gras line twice. I've been to the Mardi Gras line twice. Steve Deville was he running at the end? Yeah.
And uh... There's a girls show now, but I remember they had music there.
We uh...we played there and one time I played with Albert and the group and Popper's plays again at the Pella.
That's the tough job he's doing.

Tough job. I played and that's the three jobs I remember I played in there. One night Bill Houston asked me to come to Sea Rose and you know just look at the surround. You know I had to get a little information from him on the piano too when I could. But the way he had to play as she was, well I played a few numbers for him, you know just the rest of him up. But it...I don't like that. No. I mean you'd either have to be a musician or a postman. In other words you'd have to quit one.
Yeah.

Now those kind of people in that type of life, I don't like it. Uh...my wife said she wasn't too much for me. She never liked me to be a musician that would play every night. I'd gone into it because I...so interested one time, I bought me a method, Hannan's method. Oh yeah. It was a different exercise and I was doing it. I was doing it fine. I could read that sheet music and what they wanted me to do. I used to buy all the sheet music and I'd get the melody. And they'd improvise the chords, the chords are written on there too. Well I know the chords on the piano. Right now I don't play too much but I can play, but I've changed my style altogether. I don't play like that anymore. I try to play more modern, you see. And I've asked the boys like Howard Davis, well he'd write his part, his saxophone part. Alvin could play his part by transposing from the piano, you know. So I'd always get in there. I would need it. After Alvin first and I learned the chords, well we knew it, you see. And at that time we were playing, it's a funny thing, most of the songs they had then, they would have had what you would call a minor vamp, you know, that would be like some F, G minor, the introduction, yeah, most of that had that naive, you could fall out in with your regular chords, you see. And I gained a whole lot of experience in playing with that group. I liked to play with that group. Anything I had in the day, I knew we were going to play, I'd come home from work, I'd take a fast, I wouldn't eat, I'd get in the bed and rest. So I wouldn't have a full summer's rest on, and be ready to play that now. And, see, we'd go out there and we'd play and we'd just, we all had to wait the next week, so we'd get us right home. We wouldn't be like summer stars, you know what summer stars do, you'd run a job and
bum around all the rest of the night. Yeah, I couldn't do it.

So, I mean, after that group broke up, I lost inches. I played a couple of times with a Tiffany Cates fan, he needed a piano player, asked me could I come help him out. I told him, Sidney, well you know I'm not playing anymore. He said, well come on, you can sing, maybe, just come on out and help me. He had a ball to play, and he said he needed a piano player. I don't know what happened to his regular piano player, so I went out and I played a couple times with him. But his group was all nice bunch of friendly stars and everything like that, but I mean, when you get used to playing, you like to get accustomed to the guys that you're around. Now, at one time, I had a bass player playing with me, Jim Davis. He used to play guitar.
He's playing with Fat Domino now.

A little short fella, he's playing bass with Fat Domino. Boy, he was a terrific bass player and a terrific help to me. He could stand right here, and after I played a few boards of a number, he said, next time you come around here, I want to tell you something. So, he said, now, instead of you making straight D, change the position and make it D minor. Let your F be right in the middle. I mean, all those kind of things he was telling you. Hear all those things. And he knew I could do it, because he told me, oh, he'd doubt me there'd be a whole lot better piano player if you just try, but you won't practice. I said, Jim, I just don't, you know, I mean, I didn't have any interest in it, because I had a decent job, and that night life, and trying to work all day, there's some of the cause in the post office that's doing it now, I don't remember. Kimball.
Yeah, we haven't interviewed him yet, we must see him.
Yeah, Kimball. Another fella that plays trumpet too, used to find him, Gilbert.
Oh, is there, I don't remember, is there no? Vernon Gilbert, I didn't know he was in there. Is he a medicare?
Yeah, he's a medicare. I didn't know. Now, Gilbert Young is in there too, but he's a male handler, and I mean, but he's still playing. And, uh, what's Thornton's first name?
There's an old man that we interviewed, Mr. Boullier. Boullier, yeah. He was in the folks' office service for the years.
Yeah, at one time, yes he was. But now, a lot of those guys, uh, how they do it during the ball carnival season, I don't know how they do it.
Yeah, I don't know.

They play from ten to two, and they're right on the job the next day. Well, I tell you, that's kind of tough. Yeah. And I had a whole lot of easy in the lobby was either. I'm on the parts of the post-truck, see? It used to be my route around, uh, Josephine Louise's house, Warren's house, and all those places. That was my route for about eight years, and he changed me, put me up above Calvin Edmund. Well, I admit I had it just as easy, but it was very nice on there because I could get plenty of weight musically, you know? And at that time, that's between forty-five and fifty-five. Well, let's say that's from fifteen to fifteen to six years ago. Yeah. That does make a difference in your life, you know? I mean, I was younger. Did you quit then about six years ago?
Well, I tell you, you know, I kept on playing every chance I'd get.

I wouldn't play too much. I mean, go out looking for jobs, somebody called me, asked me to play, I would play. But, uh, the Musicians Union would give me what they call a project. Once or twice a year, so they claim that you can help you to pay your dues, but I mean, I have to pay my dues. I still belong to the Musicians Union, because they got a $1,000 policy. I wouldn't turn that down.
Oh yeah, the president. There's a lot of fellows to keep that.

But, uh, I was unfortunate, I had a heart attack in July of last year. So, they called me while I was recuperating, around the end of the siege, asking me to go play a project at the very, uh, Dajon's going this evening, up at the Trader Hospital on the third floor. Man, I was anxious to go. I wanted to get out there again. But the boss said no. No, well.
And I became discouraged.
But I did like to play the piano, and, uh, before I got older I used to like to sing, and play. You don't look old, you're not old yet.
No, I know, but I mean, uh. Fif hundred to fifty-two, about? Fifty-two, yeah. But I mean, uh, the reflexes are gone, you know. Oh yeah, in some respects you're losing.

And, now, most interest I have, the most interest I have in that little girl, my sister is teaching her to play since October. She has her playing almost a whole song of Mighty Like a Rose, since October. Yeah. And I'm fighting her too, see, because I mean, the little I know about it, I'm helping her. Yeah. But, uh, I'll tell you, I'll tell you, what I wanted to do, if I could have done it, I would like to have gone away with a big bang. I was crazy about it one time, because after I got, uh, found out I could read it off the stage, and there wasn't anything to it, I knew the changes, and the different phrases, and the different signals. I got used to it, and I liked it. I wanted to go over there, my mother wouldn't let me go. She told me no. I wanted, uh, at one time I think I could have gone away with Robert Clark, when he had the brown button. But, uh, he asked me, did I want to go, and I started to go against my mother's wishes, and I said, I know if something happens, maybe, you know, it wouldn't have been the best thing to do. So, I tell you, I, uh, I stayed around town, and I used to listen to those big bands, and I liked, I liked what you would call good music, and I understand the phrases, you know, the different orchestras, like Garland Ballers bands, and, and, and, and the melody, uh,
ballers, all.
Yeah, I mean, I like, for instance, like, Flanagan, you remember the Flanagan?
Yeah, yeah, had a big band, yeah.

With those six saxophones? Ralph Flanagan. Ralph Flanagan, six saxophones, four trumboons, and four trombones. Yeah. Boy, they were really hit. And that's the kind of music I like, that's the kind of band I would be with. Not where the piano would be, like, Aragorn, or some of those guys would be the showman, I like to hear that, that, uh, the noise section.
Uh-huh.

And they have about four mics, as we call them, with them, you know, four violins? Oh, yeah. Mice, as they're here on the mic. Now, the, I went to the auditorium one time, and that co came here with, uh, Sarah Vaughan, and I said, what's the name of that band that he came in with?
Billy Eckstein was written for a while, or?

Yeah, but no, this was a fella, he was, he made, he made Padida famous. After Duke made it, this guy made it. This guy had six trumpets, six trombones, and six sax and a baritone. And, Mr., you should've heard that band. He was a trumpet player himself. He made, uh, September song famous, too.
Oh, what's that guy's name?

He had a funny name, but man, and he, and he, something else he played. He played that Russian concerto, Walsall concerto. Boy, that, with those, with all those horns, you should've heard that band, hit them. Now, I would've liked to have been right up on that piano, but that kind of band, that's the kind of music I like, see? Now, what they're playing now, I don't like it. Uh, a lot of it is junk. I like, uh, a good melody. I like to hear somebody playing. You can tell what they're playing. Anybody can tell what they're playing if they knew the song. Some of the fellas that they're playing, you don't know what they're playing.
You say you changed your style, uh, how did you, how did you change?

Well, you ever heard Joe Robichaud play? Yes. I used to play like Joe Robichaud. That was, that's the man who taught. But I changed more, more modern because the fellas were telling me that the way I was playing, it was hard, with a small combo, see? For me to play like that.
